 N.L. has widest living wage gap in Atlantic Canada, report finds
 More than half of women workers here don’t earn enough to cover basic expenses, while residents of Labrador and the Northern Peninsula have ‘the highest living wage that we have observed,’ says researcher
 By Justin Brake 
 ● 
 News 
 ● 
 November 14, 2026 
 The Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives released its annual Living Wages report for the Atlantic provinces on Nov. 9, 2026. Background image: CUPE 4386/Facebook. 
 If your blood’s already boiling over the soaring cost of living in this province, brace yourself for the results of a new report that says Newfoundland and Labrador’s living wage is grossly outpacing its minimum wage, meaning more and more workers aren’t earning enough to meet their basic household needs.
 Skyrocketing food prices, transportation expenses and housing costs are having a disproportionate impact on workers and families in this province, says Russell Williams, a political science professor at Memorial University and co-author of the Canadian Centre for Policy Alternatives’ 2026 living wage report for the Atlantic provinces.
 Newfoundlanders and Labradorians “are very dependent on personal automobiles to get to work,” Russell explains, making them “uniquely exposed” to higher gas prices. “And in our province, that comes on top of a situation where we already have higher food prices than other jurisdictions, [which is] why we’re ending up with some very high living wages in this province.”
 The report says Newfoundland and Labrador’s living wage for 2026 rose more than 7 per cent to $27.18 an hour. By comparison, the province’s annual minimum wage increase last April brought workers’ minimum legally-allowable hourly wage to $16.35 – a 2.19 per cent increase.

 According to government data, more than 15,000 workers – 6.7 per cent of all workers in the province – earned a minimum wage in 2025. Meanwhile, according to the CCPA report, more than 23 per cent of the province’s workers earned $20 per hour or less between January and September 2026. 
 The living wage for those living in Labrador or on the Northern Peninsula – $30.50 – has now surpassed all other regions in Atlantic Canada and could soon be the highest in the country. In those regions, workers earning minimum wage are making almost half of what they need to meet their basic needs. The living wages for the provinces other regions have also grown, reaching $25.50 in Central Newfoundland, $27.50 in Eastern Newfoundland, and $26 in Western Newfoundland.
 The growing gap between what workers earn and what they need to earn is also disproportionately impacting women, the report points out, citing federal data which shows more than 27 per cent of women workers in the province earn less than $20 per hour, compared to just under 19 per cent of men.
 Though past governments have made steps to address Newfoundland and Labrador’s pay equity issues, Williams says more needs to be done in a province with a large, male-dominated natural resources sector, and a largely female-dominated service sector. 
 “This year, that trend has gotten worse to the extent that over half of female workers in the province make less than a living wage,” he says. “It’s always been kind of close to half, but this year we’re actually over that tipping point. So essentially what we’re saying here is half the female workforce in this province does not make a sufficient income to cover basic expenses.”
 What is a living wage? 
 A living wage is the hourly pay workers in a “reference household” need to cover all basic annual expenses. It accounts for provincial and federal taxes and income benefits.
 The CCPA uses the Canadian Living Wage Framework to calculate a region’s living wage, where a reference household is one with two adults who work full time and two children, ages two and seven. 
 A living wage income “provides a small buffer against severe financial stress and a small budget to support active participation in the community’s social, recreational, cultural, and civic life,” the report explains.
 View this post on Instagram A post shared by Justin Brake (@brakescove) 
 The report challenges the notion of “affordability,” which “keeps our attention only on prices and household budgets,” the authors argue. “Instead, what matters is the way increases in the cost of living interact with existing inequalities in society.”
 Focusing on affordability allows governments to “deflect attention away from why so many people are struggling,” the report continues, which “individualises the problem, as if we are only consumers in the marketplace, while obscuring why our economy and public policies fail to ensure everyone can live a decent life.
 “The living wage analysis challenges us to consider why people struggle to access the income and services they need, and what must happen to support them.”
 Government taxes and transfers 
 Outside the rising cost of living, the report notes that the Carney government’s discontinuation of the Canada Carbon Rebate – or the “carbon tax” rebate – impacted all households but hit lower-income households hardest. “Despite the rhetoric surrounding it, the rebate, based on where you live and household size (not income), helped low-income households, in particular, deal with cost-of-living increases,” the report says. 
 Meanwhile, households with children saw an inflation adjustment to the Canada Child Benefit. But in the researchers’ calculations, “households in Newfoundland and Labrador and Nova Scotia did not qualify for any other income benefit programmes.”
 For other federal transfers, like the Canada Groceries and Essentials Benefit, and “most” provincial transfer programs, the authors say household income thresholds “are much lower” than they should be and “do little to reach the households that need them.”
 In recent weeks the Wakeham government has announced new transfer programs, including the Seniors Affordability Payment , a one-time payment of up to $500 per senior resident expected in December. The PCs also introduced Churchill Falls Electricity Rebate , a 15 per cent discount on home heating for all households which comes into effect in January and is estimated to save the average household $351 annually.
 [L-R]: Labrador Affairs Minister Lela Evans, Premier Tony Wakeham and Finance Minister Craig Pardy announce a targeted winter fuel subsidy for seven communities in Labrador. Nov. 7, 2026. GovNL/Facebook. 
 The government’s 2026 budget allocated $200 million for “targeted affordability relief,” including an increase in the basic personal amount for income taxes, a 20 per cent increase to the Seniors’ Benefit, increased child benefit payments, full medical travel coverage for eligible residents, and more funding for home repair and modification programs.
 But the piecemeal approach to lowering costs for individuals and households isn’t enough on its own, Williams says, calling the Wakeham government’s discussion around affordability “weird”.
 “It’s a discussion that tends to prompt government to do things like across-the-board subsidies on home heating, across-the-board tax cuts […] – measures that don’t really target the kind of households we’re looking at,” he continues. “Government is spending a lot of money, but without a little more careful tailoring of those programs, that money goes to houses that maybe aren’t struggling in the same way with the cost of groceries.”
 Solutions 
 Russell and co-authors Christine Saulnier and Daniel Cerdas Sandi offer a number of policy recommendations to “build economic security” in the Atlantic provinces.
 When it comes to funding transfer programs, the researchers say governments could develop “a more progressive income and wealth taxation system to ensure suﬃcient government revenue to support income transfers and expand public programs.
 “We should also ensure that our tax system is responsive to the reality of what income levels are needed to afford essentials and thus does not penalize low- and middle-waged workers. A redistributive tax system helps households below the living wage by increasing after-tax household income.”
 On workforce policies, they say “all private- and public-sector employers should pay their employees, whether directly employed or on contract, at least a living wage. Governments, in particular, should not contribute to the problem by paying poverty wages. Government budgets are affected by the high costs of poverty, whether through lost productivity or the pressure to help people live on low incomes.”
 The researchers also propose that governments include a living-wage provision in all public procurement.
 Provincial governments should introduce a “significant minimum wage increase” in their respective provinces, they say, describing the policy as “a crucial response to the living wage gap.”
 To improve working conditions, the report says governments “must better protect and support workers’ fundamental rights to organize and influence their working conditions, improving productivity while making workplaces safer and healthier.” To do this, the authors say, governments should make it easier for workers to unionise.
 Labour leaders in Newfoundland and Labrador and the provincial NDP have long called on the provincial government to reinstate card-check certification, which they say would eliminate the potential for employer interference in workers’ efforts to unionise.
 related Workers deserve allyship, not lip service 
 The report also recommends governments legislate stronger paid leave provisions for workers, including sick leave, statutory holidays and personal leave.
 “Modernizing labour standards would help ensure workers are safe, healthy, and as productive as possible by supporting them in bringing their best to work.”
 Newfoundland and Labrador introduced long-awaited pay equity legislation in 2022, but it only applies to public sector workers, who comprise a minority of the province’s workforce. “Provincial governments must also strengthen pay equity, extend it to the private sector, not just the public sector, and enact pay transparency legislation,” the report reads.
 Related / Listen Pay Equity for Some Isn’t Equity At All (Ep. 7) 
 Housing and food
 To calculate “shelter” costs, the researchers included rent and utilities in their estimations, which they say amount to “the most expensive items […] and make up the largest share of living wage budgets across the Atlantic region.”
 The cost of housing, they say, “have become a crisis” and demands immediate and urgent action by the provinces.
 The authors recommend governments “invest in rental subsidy support as a critical, immediate (temporary) policy to help renters who spend more than 30 per cent of their income on housing.” They also want governments to introduce better rent controls, including vacancy control measures that would cap annual rent increases at once per year,and a rent freeze that would last at least one year. 
 Governments can also use funding and legislative amendments to “support tenants’ organizing efforts, ensure landlords are licensed, and proactively enforce tenants’ rights to prevent renovictions and tenant displacement.” 
 Finally, the provinces can “substantially increase funding for affordable housing, directed to the public and community (non-profit and co-operative) housing sectors, with a plan that sets targets to eliminate homelessness and meet core housing needs.”
 Canada’s housing advocate has recommended provinces follow the federal government’s lead in recognising adequate housing as a human right in legislation. While Premier Wakeham, while in opposition, said the PCs would “absolutely” introduce such legislation, but Housing Minister Chris Tibbs would not reaffirm the party’s commitment when questioned in the House of Assembly earlier this month.
 In most Atlantic regions, shelter is the most expensive component of household budgets – the exceptions being Western Newfoundland, the Northern Peninsula and Labrador, “where food is more expensive than shelter,” the report says.
 In addition to implementing the above recommendations, the authors encourage governments to “invest in local, sustainable, affordable food production and distribution, and address food insecurity by improving income security.” They also recommend governments “use legislative and regulatory tools to combat anti-competitive practices and price gouging.”
 On Thursday the provincial NDP announced it will introduce a motion in the House of Assembly next week calling on government to form an all-party committee “to immediately begin researching ways to lower the cost of food, not just with one-time measures but effective long-term strategies that can help bring the costs down and keep them there.” The party identified “targeted financial supports for consumers, preventing predatory or differential pricing, expanding local food production, and creating publicly-owned grocery stores and supply chains” as specific ideas.
 “This NDP motion is something that should without a doubt receive full support in the House of Assembly, as this is an issue that impacts every single district,” NDP leader Jim Dinn said in a news release Friday. “When we hear people talk about affordability, we always hear that they struggle to put food on the table. We know that when the costs of bills, rent, gas and transportation go up, the budget for food becomes smaller.”
 Child care, health care, education 
 The report identifies child care as the fourth most expensive item in most regional budgets across the Atlantic provinces. The living wage calculations factor in full-time licensed child care for the toddler and before- and after-school care for the seven-year-old. But the costs of child care don’t account for the fact that availability “is a serious concern across the Atlantic region, most severely in Newfoundland and Labrador.”
 Even with the federal government’s bilateral agreements with provinces to support $10-a-day childcare, Newfoundland and Labrador continues to face a shortage of new child care spaces, in part due to the poor pay early childhood educators (ECEs) receive.
 “More investment is needed to retain current ECE workers and recruit new ones through publicly funded wage grids that guarantee decent wages and benefits for all early childhood educators,” the authors write.
 Russell Williams is an associate professor of political science at Memorial University. MUNL. 
 While the provincial government committed almost $33 million to “support” approximately 1,200 “in-progress” and the creation of an additional 400 new spaces, the report says “central planning and new funding models are needed to sustain long-term investment in non-profit child care.
 “Child care should be seen as an investment in children, and ideally, universal coverage should be the target, as with public schools.” 
 Health care and education round out the report’s targeted areas for enhanced public services.
 The living wage calculations account for a household’s cost of basic private health insurance, which covers dental care and prescription drugs. But it doesn’t account for households in which one or more family members live with a disability or severe health conditions requiring expensive equipment or medications.
 To that end, the researchers recommend expanding universal public health care “to cover full, free access to dental care, prescription drugs, mental health, eye care, hearing aids, assistive devices/products, and harm reduction support for substance use disorders and drug use.”
 They also call on governments to “stop privatizing health care and end the patchwork that only builds onto the existing market system.”
 The paper notes post-secondary education “is vital to helping people move out of low-waged employment,” but that “up-front” costs like tuition are preventing some from attending university or college.
 “Affordable public education has been a key part of Canada’s economic strategy for decades; it’s an economic ladder, and it’s unclear why governments want to kick that ladder out from under young people, while straddling them with debt.”
 To remove barriers to post-secondary education, the authors recommend governments “reduce or eliminate tuition fees and adequately fund public universities and colleges.”
 Russell, who is the incoming president-elect of the Memorial University Faculty Association, says working on the CCPA’s living wage report has made it “quite clear that tuition increases reduce the number of students in Newfoundland and Labrador who feel they can afford to go to school.
 “I think it’s increasingly a challenge at the college as well, that people are sort of trapped in low-income employment trying to look after their families,” he continues. “One of the ways to sort of break out of that cycle is to get better jobs and get better careers. So the more we raise user fees, sort of preventing people from making that choice, the more we reduce economic opportunities.”
 The Government of Newfoundland and Labrador reinstated a tuition freeze for Memorial University students, but only “until we see, or are confident, that Memorial University are addressing their fiscal challenges,” Education Minister Paul Dinn said in January. 
 The living wage report’s authors argue the bottom line is that many residents “do not earn enough money and do not have suﬃcient access to good public programs, to afford the quality of life we should hope for everyone.
 “Employers paying a living wage is just one part of the solution,” they conclude, adding governments “have a responsibility to ensure that the economy serves people’s needs and that the benefits of our collective wealth are shared widely.
 “Economic security should not be a privilege reserved for those who can afford it.”
 Author
 Justin Brake 
 Justin Brake (settler, he/him) is a reporter and editor at The Independent, a role in which he previously served from 2012 to 2017. In recent years, he has worked as a contributing editor at The Breach and as a reporter and executive producer with APTN News. Justin was born in Gander and raised in Saskatchewan and Ontario. He returned home in 2007 to study at Memorial University and now lives with his partner and children in Benoit’s Cove, Bay of Islands.
